transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um... well, I'm here because things have just been getting really, really difficult at work lately. I work as a therapist—mostly behavioral stuff, working with my clients day to day—and honestly, it's starting to scare me a little because I just can't keep my head clear anymore. It's like my brain is full of cotton or something. 

I'll be right in the middle of a session, right? And the client is talking or doing something I need to track, and I just completely lose track of what they're saying. The words go in my ears, but nothing happens in my head. And the paperwork... man, the paperwork is an absolute nightmare now. I have to do these chart notes at the end of the day, and I'll find myself just staring at the screen, rereading the exact same chart note over and over and over again. I'll read a sentence five times and still not know what it said. 

And then, if I have to make a decision—just simple, everyday decisions about a client's plan or what to do next, stuff that I used to handle on autopilot without even blinking—I just freeze. I completely freeze up and my mind goes totally blank. It's just so frustrating because I know how to do my job, I've done it a hundred times, but my brain just won't cooperate right now, and I really need to figure out what's going on before I mess something up.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with your work?

Well, um... if I really think back on it, trying to pinpoint exactly when it started getting this bad... I'd say it's been going on for about a month now. Yeah, right around a month. Because, see, what happened was our clinic had this sudden turnover. We lost a couple of key staff members all at once—one moved out of state, another went on unexpected medical leave—and it just threw everything into absolute chaos. 

And because I'm one of the younger guys there, you know, just 20, they kind of leaned on me to pick up the slack. So my schedule got completely upended. I went from having a pretty predictable daytime routine to suddenly having to cover all these late-evening shifts. And it's not just the hours, it's the type of work that comes with those hours. The evening shifts are when we get a lot more of the acute stuff, the crisis interventions. 

So suddenly I'm dealing with these really heavy, intense client situations late at night, and the paperwork for crisis stuff is just... it's a whole different beast. It's so much heavier, so much more detailed, and there's so much liability attached to it. You have to document every single little thing to make sure you're covered and the client is safe. And that's exactly when I started noticing the brain fog, you know? Sitting there at 9:00 PM, staring at a crisis assessment form, trying to write down what just happened, and realizing I couldn't hold a single thought in my head. It's been like that every single day for the last four weeks, just this constant, uphill battle where I'm trying to push through the evening, and the harder I try to focus on the paperwork, the more my brain just completely shuts down on me.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time since you started experiencing these work difficulties?

Well, um... sad? I don't know if "sad" is really the right word for it. It's not like I'm sitting around crying or anything like that. It's more just... I don't know, maybe frustrated? Or just completely drained. Like, I'll get home from one of those late shifts I was telling you about, right? And I'll just sit on the edge of my bed, still in my work clothes, and I just feel this heavy... nothingness. 

But I wouldn't say I'm walking around feeling depressed or down in the dumps all day. It's just that everything feels like such a massive chore now. Like, even just the idea of getting up and making dinner feels like climbing a mountain, so I just don't do it. I just sit there. But sad? No, I don't think I've really been feeling sad. It's more just this overwhelming sense of being stuck and not knowing how to fix my brain so I can just do my job again. Because I used to be really good at it, you know? I really cared about my clients, and now I just... I just feel like I'm failing them, which sucks, but it's not sadness, exactly. Does that make sense?
Have you been feeling anxious or on edge since your work difficulties started?

Anxious? Um... well, I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by anxious. Like, I'm not having panic attacks or anything. My heart isn't racing out of my chest, and I'm not, you know, hyperventilating in the supply closet at work. But... am I on edge? Yeah, I guess you could say that. But it's entirely because of the work stuff. 

Like I was saying before, about the crisis interventions and the liability? It's just... it's a lot of pressure. When you're sitting across from someone who is actively suicidal, or they're having a severe manic episode, and it's 10:00 PM and you're the only one there who can handle it... you have to be on your game. You have to make the right call, right then and there. And because my brain is doing this weird fog thing, I'm constantly second-guessing myself. 

So I'll be in the session, and instead of just listening and responding naturally like I used to, I'm sitting there thinking, "Okay, did I ask the right question? Did I miss a red flag? Am I documenting this correctly in my head so I can write it down later?" And then I get out of the session, and I'm staring at the computer screen, and I'm just so tense. Like my shoulders are practically up to my ears. Because I know that if I mess up that paperwork, if I forget to document that we did a safety plan, and then something happens to that client... that's on me. That's my license, that's my job, that's someone's life. 

So yeah, I'm definitely tense and on edge when I'm at the clinic, but it's not like this free-floating anxiety, you know? It's very specific to the fact that I can't think straight and I'm terrified I'm going to make a massive mistake because of it. And then I come home, and I'm just so exhausted from being that tense for eight hours straight that I just collapse. So I don't know if that counts as being anxious, exactly, but I'm definitely stressed out about the whole situation.
Have you been avoiding certain tasks or situations at work because of your difficulties with concentration and decision-making?

Well, um... avoiding tasks? I guess... I mean, I wouldn't say I'm hiding in the bathroom or anything to get out of doing things, but... it's more like I just couldn't keep pretending I was handling it all. The decision-making thing, like I was saying before, it got to a point where it wasn't just me being stressed or taking longer to write my notes. It was actually starting to bleed into the sessions themselves, and that's the one thing I promised myself I would never let happen. 

Like, there was this one night last week, I had a client who was really escalating, and usually, I'd know exactly how to de-escalate, exactly what protocols to follow, but I just... I froze. I was sitting there, and my mind went completely blank, and I was hesitating on every single word I said. And the client noticed, you know? They could tell I wasn't fully there, that I wasn't confident in what I was doing. And that's dangerous. In this field, if you hesitate when someone is in crisis, it can go south so incredibly fast. 

So after that session, I just sat in my office for like an hour, staring at the wall, and I realized I couldn't keep doing this. I couldn't keep putting my clients at risk because my brain refuses to cooperate. So... I actually went to my supervisor the next morning. I just walked into her office and I told her, "Look, I need help." I had to admit that my mistakes, the hesitation, the brain fog... it was all starting to affect client care. And I told her straight up that I just didn't trust myself to keep working safely, not without being evaluated or figuring out what the hell is wrong with me. Because if I make a wrong call, it's not like messing up a spreadsheet, you know? It's someone's life. So yeah, I guess I'm avoiding the work in the sense that I literally had to ask them to pull me back because I knew I wasn't safe to practice right now.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Weight? Um... well, I haven't actually stepped on a scale or anything, so I don't have an exact number for you. But... yeah, I definitely think I have. It's just... eating hasn't really been happening much lately. 

It's like my stomach just completely forgot how to tell my brain that it's empty. Most days, I honestly just don't feel hungry at all. I can go practically the whole day and it doesn't even cross my mind until someone actually reminds me to eat. Like, my roommate will come home from his shift and ask what I had for lunch, and I'll stop and realize I've literally had nothing but a cup of coffee since I woke up. I'm just skipping meals without really meaning to, you know? It's not like I'm doing it on purpose or trying to diet or anything like that. It's just that the thought of food doesn't even register, or if it does, the effort of actually making something just feels so exhausting that I don't bother. 

And I know I must be dropping pounds because my clothes aren't fitting right anymore. Like, I was getting dressed to go into the office a few days ago, and my work pants—the ones I wear all the time—they've gotten so loose. They were literally sliding down my hips. I had to go dig through my closet to find a belt just so I wouldn't look completely unprofessional if I had to stand up in front of a client. So, yeah, I haven't weighed myself, but I'm definitely losing weight just from unintentionally skipping meals all the time.
Have you been having trouble sleeping since your work difficulties started?

Sleep? Oh man, sleep is... sleep is just a whole other nightmare right now, honestly. It's so frustrating because, like I said, I come home from the clinic and I am just bone-tired. I mean, physically and mentally exhausted from being so tense and second-guessing every single thing I did for eight hours straight. My body feels like it weighs a thousand pounds, and all I want to do is just crash. 

But then... I actually get into bed, and it's like my brain suddenly decides it's time to run a marathon. I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling in the dark, and my mind just starts replaying the entire day on a loop. I'll think about that crisis intervention, and I'll start analyzing every word I said, wondering if I missed a cue, wondering if I documented the safety plan right. I'll literally lie there for hours, tossing and turning, just completely unable to shut my brain off. It's like I'm so exhausted, but my mind refuses to let me rest because it's too busy panicking about whether I ruined someone's life that day.

And the worst part is, even when I do finally manage to drift off—usually because I'm just too exhausted to stay awake anymore—it's not even good sleep. It's like this restless, shallow kind of sleep. And then, without fail, I'll wake up way before my alarm is supposed to go off. Like, I'll jolt awake at 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning, and my heart is already beating a little faster, and I just know I'm not going back to sleep. So I just lie there again, waiting for the sun to come up, feeling like I barely slept at all. I wake up feeling just as exhausted, if not more exhausted, than when I went to bed. So yeah, sleep has been really, really bad lately. It's just this vicious cycle of being exhausted, not being able to sleep, and then being even more exhausted the next day.
Have you been enjoying the things you used to like doing before your work difficulties started?

Enjoying things? Um, no. Not really. Honestly, not at all. It's... it's actually really depressing to think about, because I used to have all these things I loved doing, things that would help me decompress after a long week at the clinic. Like, I've played guitar since I was in middle school, right? I used to pick it up almost every evening, just strumming, trying to learn new fingerpicking patterns, or just playing stuff I knew by heart. It was my way of winding down. But now... my guitar has literally just been sitting in the corner of my bedroom for weeks. It's gathering dust. I look at it, and I just feel... nothing. Or I feel like it would take too much energy to even lift it out of the stand, let alone actually play anything. 

And it's not just the guitar. I've been playing in this casual weekend soccer league with some buddies for a couple of years now. We play every Sunday morning, and it used to be the highlight of my week. Just running around, getting some fresh air, hanging out with the guys. But lately, I just keep bailing on them. Every Saturday night, I'll text the group chat and make up some excuse about feeling under the weather or having too much paperwork to catch up on, which is a lie, obviously. I just can't bring myself to go out there and pretend to care about a game. 

Same thing with the animal shelter. I used to volunteer there on Wednesday evenings, walking the dogs, cleaning out the cages, just spending time with them. I love animals, and it always felt good to help out. But I haven't been in over a month. I keep telling the coordinator I have scheduling conflicts, but the truth is I just don't have it in me. 

Even the basic stuff I used to enjoy, like cooking a nice dinner for myself or going for a hike on a Saturday afternoon... it's all just gone. A few weekends ago, I tried to force myself to go on this trail I used to love, thinking maybe being out in nature would snap me out of it. But I was just walking along, looking at the trees, and it just felt like I was going through the motions. There was no joy in it, no sense of peace or relaxation. It just felt pointless, like, why am I even out here walking in a circle? So yeah, everything I used to like doing just feels completely empty now. I don't get any enjoyment out of any of it anymore.
Have you been feeling worthless or like you're a failure in any way since your work difficulties started?

Worthless? Yeah... yeah, that's pretty much exactly the word for it. It's just this constant, heavy feeling that I'm completely failing at everything I'm supposed to be doing. It's so hard to even talk about because I know how important the work at the clinic is, and these people are coming to us in crisis, relying on us to be on top of things. But lately, my brain just completely spirals over the smallest things. 

Like, we have to document everything, obviously, and if I realize I missed just one single detail in a note—like, maybe I forgot to jot down a specific resource I gave someone, or I didn't summarize a conversation perfectly—I just sit there staring at the computer screen, and I keep telling myself that I am completely useless. I'll literally sit there at my desk and just berate myself, thinking, 'How could you forget that? You're terrible at this, you shouldn't even be in this field.' 

And it's the exact same thing with the phone calls. The front desk will leave me a message to call a client back, and if I forget to return that call right away... like, if I get sidetracked and don't call them back for an hour, or God forbid, I have to wait until the next morning... the guilt just eats me alive. I'll be driving home, gripping the steering wheel, just tearing myself apart over it. I just have this overwhelming feeling that I'm letting the clients down, you know? They need help, they reach out, and I can't even manage to return a simple phone call on time. 

And it's not just the clients. I feel like I'm letting everyone at the clinic down, too. My supervisor, my coworkers... they're all working so hard, juggling their own massive caseloads, and I'm just dragging the whole team down by messing up these basic tasks. Every time I walk into the office, I just feel like a total fraud, like everyone must be looking at me and realizing how incompetent I am. I just feel like I'm doing more harm than good just by being there.
Have you been having any thoughts about death or wanting to harm yourself lately?

Harm myself? No, no, I... I don't have a plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I really don't. But... man, it's hard to even say this out loud, especially given what I do for a living. But lately, usually when I'm lying there in the dark after barely sleeping, or when I'm just so exhausted I can't even think straight and the guilt is just eating away at me... I keep having these thoughts. These really heavy thoughts that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. 

Like, if I could just go to sleep and the alarm wouldn't go off, and I wouldn't have to face the clinic or the clients or the constant feeling that I'm messing everything up. It just feels like it would be a relief, you know? Just... quiet. No more overthinking, no more letting people down. And I want to be really clear, I'm not sitting around trying to figure out how to make that happen. I'm not planning anything or looking for a way out like that. 

But the fact that the thought keeps creeping in... it honestly terrifies me. It scares me so much because I know exactly what that can mean. I mean, I sit across from people at the clinic who say those exact same words to me, and I know the protocols, I know the risk assessments we have to run. I know the trajectory of what it means when someone starts wishing they wouldn't wake up. So catching myself thinking that way... it's just this massive red flag in my own brain, and it makes me panic. Because it's like, how did I get here? How am I the one having these thoughts now? It just makes me feel even more broken, realizing that my mind is actually going to that dark of a place, even if I don't intend to act on it. It's just... it's really, really scary to be on this side of it, knowing what I know.
Are you still able to experience pleasure or interest in activities that you previously found enjoyable?

Well, like I was saying before, it's just... it's all completely gone. I mean, my guitar, right? It's just sitting there in the corner of my room. I haven't touched it in weeks. And it's not just that I don't have time, it's that I look at it and I just... I don't care. I don't have the energy to even pick it up. And the soccer league... I keep bailing on them. Every single weekend, I'm making up some excuse about why I can't make it to the game. Same with the animal shelter, I just stopped going. I haven't been in over a month. 

And it's even the little things, you know? Like, I used to love cooking a nice meal for myself, taking the time to chop up all the ingredients, try a new recipe... now I just can't be bothered. Or hiking! I told you about that hike I tried to go on, right? I forced myself to go out to that trail I used to love, thinking maybe, just maybe, being out in the woods would make me feel something. But I was just walking along, and it felt so incredibly pointless. Like I was just going through the motions, putting one foot in front of the other, but there was no joy in it at all. It just felt like a chore. So, yeah, everything I used to enjoy... it just feels completely empty now. I don't get anything out of any of it anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family since you started experiencing these difficulties?

Relationships... yeah. I mean, I haven't really noticed any big changes, honestly. It's not like we're getting into massive fights or anything like that. But, well, I guess... I mean, I'm just not really around as much, you know? Like I was saying with the soccer league and the animal shelter, I'm just kind of pulling back from everything, and I guess that includes people, too. 

Like, my mom will call me, and usually, we'd talk for, I don't know, forty-five minutes on a Sunday, just catching up on everything going on with her and my dad, and I'd tell her about work... but now, when I see her name pop up on my phone, I just stare at it. I just let it ring and go to voicemail because the thought of having to put on that happy voice and pretend everything is fine... it's just exhausting. I can't do it. And then I'll text her back like two days later saying I was just super busy at the clinic or something, which just adds to that whole pile of guilt I was talking about earlier. 

And my friends... man, my buddies from high school, we have this group chat, right? And they're always firing off memes and making plans to go grab a drink or watch the game or whatever. And I used to be right in the middle of it. But lately, I'll see the notifications piling up—like, thirty unread messages—and I don't even open the chat. I just swipe it away. A couple of them have reached out individually, like, 'Hey man, you good? Haven't seen you around,' and I just give them the same excuse. 'Just tired, work is crazy.' 

So, I wouldn't say the relationships have changed in the sense that they're mad at me or we're arguing, but... I guess I'm just kind of ghosting my own life. I'm just not participating in any of those connections anymore because I don't have the energy, and honestly, I just feel like I'd be a total drag to be around anyway with how heavy my head is all the time. So I just stay in my apartment, and I guess they're just getting used to me not being there.
Do you often find yourself blaming yourself for things that happen at work or in your personal life?

Blaming myself... yeah. Honestly, it's exhausting how much I do that. It's just this constant loop, especially with work. I mean, the clinic is so fast-paced, and there's a lot to keep track of, but lately, my reaction to even the smallest mistake is just... it's so extreme. 

Like, we have to keep really meticulous records, right? And if I'm doing a write-up and I realize I missed one tiny detail in a note—maybe I forgot to document a specific phrase a client used, or I left out a minor part of their check-in—my brain just completely spirals. I don't just think, 'Oh, I made a mistake, I'll fix it.' I sit there staring at the computer screen and I just keep telling myself how completely useless I am. I'll literally be thinking, 'You're a fraud, you can't even do basic documentation right.' 

And it's the same thing with the phones. We get so many messages, and if I forget to return a call right away... even if it's only been like an hour or two because I got caught up with something else... I immediately start agonizing over it. I convince myself that I'm completely letting the clients down, that they're sitting there waiting for help and I'm failing them. And not just the clients, but everyone at the clinic. I feel like I'm letting the whole team down, like I'm this weak link that's dragging the entire practice backward. 

I know, logically, that people get busy. I know that if a coworker did the exact same thing, I'd tell them it's fine, it's just human error. But when it's me? I just can't let it go. I'll carry that one little missed detail or that one delayed phone call with me for the rest of the day, and I'll just beat myself up over it relentlessly. It just reinforces this heavy feeling that I'm messing everything up and that everyone would probably be better off if I wasn't the one handling their cases.
Do you often feel guilty or ashamed about things that aren't your fault?

Yeah, I mean, that kind of ties right back into what I was just rambling about with work, honestly. The guilt is just... it's constant. And a lot of the time, it's over stuff that I realistically couldn't even control, but the shame just completely eats me alive anyway. 

Like, I was just talking about those phone calls, right? Sometimes the clinic gets completely slammed, or our phone system glitches—which happens a lot because our software is incredibly outdated—and so I might forget to return a call right away simply because the message got buried or I was covering for someone else who called out sick. It's not my fault we're short-staffed or the system crashed. But the second I realize someone has been waiting? It doesn't matter whose fault it actually is. This massive wave of guilt just hits me. I just sit there staring at the phone and I keep telling myself I'm completely useless. I literally convince myself that I'm single-handedly letting the clients down, that they're struggling and it's entirely on my shoulders because I wasn't fast enough. 

And it's not even just the clients, it's everyone at the clinic. I feel this deep, intense shame, like I'm dragging the whole team down and ruining the practice's reputation, even though I'm just one person dealing with a broken phone system. 

And it's the exact same thing with the notes I mentioned earlier. If a client is talking a mile a minute, jumping from topic to topic, and I miss one detail in a note because I physically couldn't type fast enough to keep up... I don't give myself any grace. I don't think, 'Well, nobody could have caught all that, it's fine.' I just spiral into feeling so incredibly ashamed. I keep telling myself I'm useless and that I'm letting everyone down by not having a perfect record. It's like my brain just hoovers up all the blame in the room, even if a situation was totally out of my hands to begin with, and I just carry all that heavy guilt around with me all day. I just can't seem to separate what's actually my fault from what isn't.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities outside of work due to your current state of mind?

Responsibilities outside of work... I mean, I guess I'm not totally sure what you mean by that, because honestly, I don't really have a lot of them to begin with. I'm only twenty, so it's just me living in my apartment. I don't have kids, I don't have a family to support, I don't even have a pet. I used to think about getting a dog—especially back when I was volunteering at the animal shelter like I mentioned before, I'd see these great dogs come through and think about bringing one home—but I'm so glad I didn't, because right now, the thought of having to walk a dog twice a day and make sure it's fed and happy... I just couldn't do it. 

So, because it's just me, I don't really have those kinds of heavy obligations waiting for me when I clock out. It's mostly just... the basic maintenance of being a person, I guess? Like keeping the apartment clean, doing laundry, going to the grocery store. And I wouldn't say I'm completely failing at that stuff, but I'm definitely just doing the bare minimum to survive. Like, my laundry will just sit in the basket for a week and a half, and I'll just pull wrinkled clothes out of it in the morning because I can't bring myself to actually fold anything and put it in the dresser. It just seems like this monumental, pointless task. Why even bother folding shirts when I'm just going to wear them again, you know? 

And with food... I used to be really good about meal prepping on Sundays. I'd make these big batches of chicken and rice for the week so I wouldn't have to stress about lunch at the clinic. But lately, I don't even go to the store. I just order takeout or eat whatever is sitting in the pantry, like I'll literally just have a bowl of cereal for dinner, because the thought of driving to the supermarket and walking up and down the aisles under those bright fluorescent lights with all those people... it just feels impossible. 

But I don't know if that's what you mean by responsibilities. As far as the real adult stuff goes, I've got my rent on autopay, my electric bill is on autopay, so the big things are getting taken care of automatically. I'm not getting evicted or anything. So I guess, no, I'm not really having a hard time with outside responsibilities, mostly just because I don't really have any right now. I'm just kind of going to work, coming home, and sitting on the couch until I have to go back to work again.
Are you finding that your current difficulties are affecting your ability to maintain relationships or engage in daily activities outside of work?

Relationships outside of work... I mean, like I was saying, I just go home and sit on the couch, so I'm not exactly going out of my way to see friends or hang out with anyone. I just don't have the energy to keep up with people right now. 

But honestly, my personal life being kind of non-existent isn't even the thing that's really scaring me the most. I know you're asking about outside of work, but my mind just keeps looping back to the clinic, because that's where things are really falling apart. It's one thing if I'm just ruining my own evening by sitting in the dark and ignoring my laundry, but it's entirely different when it starts impacting other people, you know? 

All that stuff I was just telling you about—the agonizing over the phone calls, the freezing up over the documentation, the constant guilt—it just kept building and building. It got so bad recently that I actually had to go and sit down with my supervisor. Which, by the way, was incredibly nerve-wracking. I hate admitting when I'm struggling, especially in a professional setting where you're supposed to be the one who has it all together for the clients. I was terrified they were going to fire me on the spot. 

But I just couldn't keep hiding it. I told my supervisor I needed help because my mistakes and all that hesitation were actually starting to affect client care. Like, I'd be so frozen trying to make sure a note was perfect that I'd delay getting a file to the next person, or I'd second-guess myself so much on the phone that I wasn't actually being helpful to the person on the other end of the line. It's the absolute last thing I want, because these people are coming to us when they're vulnerable, and I felt like a total liability. I just reached this breaking point where I told my boss I didn't trust myself to keep working safely without being evaluated. I couldn't keep going in every day pretending everything was fine when I felt like I was actively doing harm just by being so entirely unsure of myself. So, yeah, my outside life is pretty much just me isolating, but the work situation... that's what really forced my hand to come in here today.
Have you been having any thoughts about harming yourself or taking your own life, and if so, have you thought about how you would do it?

Harming myself... I mean, I want to be really clear right out of the gate that I do not have a plan to hurt myself. I haven't thought about how I would do it, I don't have a method picked out, I'm not sitting alone in my apartment looking things up or anything like that. I really want to emphasize that. 

But... and this is honestly really hard to admit out loud, especially given where I work... I keep having these thoughts. It usually happens at night, when I'm just completely drained from carrying all that guilt around all day, and I'm finally lying in bed. My mind will just start wandering, and this thought just kind of drifts in that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up the next morning. 

It's not that I want to actively do something to end my life, it's more just this overwhelming, heavy feeling of wanting to hit a permanent pause button on everything. The idea of just going to sleep and not having to wake up and face the phone ringing, or the incomplete notes, or that constant, crushing fear of letting everyone down again... it just sounds like such a relief in those moments. 

And then, almost immediately after I think it, it really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because working at the clinic, even just being around the administrative side of things, I know exactly what that can mean. I see it on the intake forms, I hear the clinicians talking about it—I know that wishing you wouldn't wake up is a massive warning sign. I know the trajectory of how those thoughts can escalate if you don't do something about them. So catching my own brain doing it, finding actual comfort in the idea of just slipping away in my sleep? It's like a massive red flag waving right in my face. I don't have a plan, but just the fact that my mind is going to that dark of a place to find an escape is a huge part of why I told my boss I needed help. It's just too scary to ignore when you know exactly what those kinds of thoughts represent.
Have your symptoms been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past few weeks?

Worse. Definitely worse. It's... well, this whole thing really started about a month ago, and it feels like it's just been snowballing ever since. See, what happened was, we lost a couple of staff members at the clinic pretty suddenly. Just, boom, people were gone, and management was completely scrambling to figure out how to cover everything. So, my schedule got completely shifted around to fill the gaps, and they moved me into this late-evening coverage. 

And the evening shifts... I mean, it's just a totally different environment. The daytime is busy, sure, but the evening is when things get really intense. You start getting all these heavy, urgent calls, so suddenly I was drowning in all this heavier crisis paperwork. And with crisis documentation, you have to be so incredibly precise, because if you miss one detail, the consequences could be disastrous. You're documenting risk assessments, safety plans, all these things where you absolutely cannot afford to make a mistake. 

So that all started about a month ago, and at first, I just thought, okay, I'm just adjusting to the new hours, I'm just tired because my sleep schedule is off and I'm getting home so late. But it didn't get better. I'll literally be thinking, 'You're a fraud, you can't even do basic documentation right.' 

And it's the same thing with the phones. We get so many messages, and if I forget to return a call right away... even if it's only been like an hour or two because I got caught up with something else... I immediately start agonizing over it. I convince myself that I'm completely letting the clients down, that they're sitting there waiting for help and I'm failing them. And not just the clients, but everyone at the clinic. I feel like I'm letting the whole team down, like I'm this weak link that's dragging the entire practice backward. 

I know, logically, that people get busy. I know that if a coworker did the exact same thing, I'd tell them it's fine, it's just human error. But when it's me? I just can't let it go. I'll carry that one little missed detail or that one delayed phone call with me for the rest of the day, and I'll just beat myself up over it relentlessly. It just reinforces this heavy feeling that I'm messing everything up and that everyone would probably be better off if I wasn't the one handling their cases.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive feelings of guilt or shame
doctor.question: Do you often feel guilty or ashamed about things that aren't your fault?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: If I miss one detail in a note or forget to return a call right away, I keep telling myself I'm useless and that I'm letting the clients and everyone at the clinic down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or shame, which directly maps to the Worthlessness/Guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, that kind of ties right back into what I was just rambling about with work, honestly. The guilt is just... it's constant. And a lot of the time, it's over stuff that I realistically couldn't even control, but the shame just completely eats me alive anyway. 

Like, I was just talking about those phone calls, right? Sometimes the clinic gets completely slammed, or our phone system glitches—which happens a lot because our software is incredibly outdated—and so I might forget to return a call right away simply because the message got buried or I was covering for someone else who called out sick. It's not my fault we're short-staffed or the system crashed. But the second I realize someone has been waiting? It doesn't matter whose fault it actually is. This massive wave of guilt just hits me. I just sit there staring at the phone and I keep telling myself I'm completely useless. I literally convince myself that I'm single-handedly letting the clients down, that they're struggling and it's entirely on my shoulders because I wasn't fast enough. 

And it's not even just the clients, it's everyone at the clinic. I feel this deep, intense shame, like I'm dragging the whole team down and ruining the practice's reputation, even though I'm just one person dealing with a broken phone system. 

And it's the exact same thing with the notes I mentioned earlier. If a client is talking a mile a minute, jumping from topic to topic, and I miss one detail in a note because I physically couldn't type fast enough to keep up... I don't give myself any grace. I don't think, 'Well, nobody could have caught all that, it's fine.' I just spiral into feeling so incredibly ashamed. I keep telling myself I'm useless and that I'm letting everyone down by not having a perfect record. It's like my brain just hoovers up all the blame in the room, even if a situation was totally out of my hands to begin with, and I just carry all that heavy guilt around with me all day. I just can't seem to separate what's actually my fault from what isn't.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities outside of work due to your current state of mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties fulfilling responsibilities outside of work. The patient's functional impairment manifestation specifically focuses on work-related issues (affecting client care, telling supervisor), and no other symptom explicitly covers responsibilities outside of work.

patient.answer:
Responsibilities outside of work... I mean, I guess I'm not totally sure what you mean by that, because honestly, I don't really have a lot of them to begin with. I'm only twenty, so it's just me living in my apartment. I don't have kids, I don't have a family to support, I don't even have a pet. I used to think about getting a dog—especially back when I was volunteering at the animal shelter like I mentioned before, I'd see these great dogs come through and think about bringing one home—but I'm so glad I didn't, because right now, the thought of having to walk a dog twice a day and make sure it's fed and happy... I just couldn't do it. 

So, because it's just me, I don't really have those kinds of heavy obligations waiting for me when I clock out. It's mostly just... the basic maintenance of being a person, I guess? Like keeping the apartment clean, doing laundry, going to the grocery store. And I wouldn't say I'm completely failing at that stuff, but I'm definitely just doing the bare minimum to survive. Like, my laundry will just sit in the basket for a week and a half, and I'll just pull wrinkled clothes out of it in the morning because I can't bring myself to actually fold anything and put it in the dresser. It just seems like this monumental, pointless task. Why even bother folding shirts when I'm just going to wear them again, you know? 

And with food... I used to be really good about meal prepping on Sundays. I'd make these big batches of chicken and rice for the week so I wouldn't have to stress about lunch at the clinic. But lately, I don't even go to the store. I just order takeout or eat whatever is sitting in the pantry, like I'll literally just have a bowl of cereal for dinner, because the thought of driving to the supermarket and walking up and down the aisles under those bright fluorescent lights with all those people... it just feels impossible. 

But I don't know if that's what you mean by responsibilities. As far as the real adult stuff goes, I've got my rent on autopay, my electric bill is on autopay, so the big things are getting taken care of automatically. I'm not getting evicted or anything. So I guess, no, I'm not really having a hard time with outside responsibilities, mostly just because I don't really have any right now. I'm just kind of going to work, coming home, and sitting on the couch until I have to go back to work again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you finding that your current difficulties are affecting your ability to maintain relationships or engage in daily activities outside of work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I told my supervisor I needed help because my mistakes and hesitation were starting to affect client care, and I didn't trust myself to keep working safely without being evaluated.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the patient's symptoms on their ability to maintain relationships and engage in daily activities, which assesses social and daily functioning (Functional Impairment).

patient.answer:
Relationships outside of work... I mean, like I was saying, I just go home and sit on the couch, so I'm not exactly going out of my way to see friends or hang out with anyone. I just don't have the energy to keep up with people right now. 

But honestly, my personal life being kind of non-existent isn't even the thing that's really scaring me the most. I know you're asking about outside of work, but my mind just keeps looping back to the clinic, because that's where things are really falling apart. It's one thing if I'm just ruining my own evening by sitting in the dark and ignoring my laundry, but it's entirely different when it starts impacting other people, you know? 

All that stuff I was just telling you about—the agonizing over the phone calls, the freezing up over the documentation, the constant guilt—it just kept building and building. It got so bad recently that I actually had to go and sit down with my supervisor. Which, by the way, was incredibly nerve-wracking. I hate admitting when I'm struggling, especially in a professional setting where you're supposed to be the one who has it all together for the clients. I was terrified they were going to fire me on the spot. 

But I just couldn't keep hiding it. I told my supervisor I needed help because my mistakes and all that hesitation were actually starting to affect client care. Like, I'd be so frozen trying to make sure a note was perfect that I'd delay getting a file to the next person, or I'd second-guess myself so much on the phone that I wasn't actually being helpful to the person on the other end of the line. It's the absolute last thing I want, because these people are coming to us when they're vulnerable, and I felt like a total liability. I just reached this breaking point where I told my boss I didn't trust myself to keep working safely without being evaluated. I couldn't keep going in every day pretending everything was fine when I felt like I was actively doing harm just by being so entirely unsure of myself. So, yeah, my outside life is pretty much just me isolating, but the work situation... that's what really forced my hand to come in here today.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal ideation with intent
doctor.question: Have you been having any thoughts about harming yourself or taking your own life, and if so, have you thought about how you would do it?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I don't have a plan to hurt myself, but I keep having these thoughts like it would be easier if I didn't wake up, and that scares me because I know what that can mean.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of self-harm or suicide and whether I have a plan, which directly corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Harming myself... I mean, I want to be really clear right out of the gate that I do not have a plan to hurt myself. I haven't thought about how I would do it, I don't have a method picked out, I'm not sitting alone in my apartment looking things up or anything like that. I really want to emphasize that. 

But... and this is honestly really hard to admit out loud, especially given where I work... I keep having these thoughts. It usually happens at night, when I'm just completely drained from carrying all that guilt around all day, and I'm finally lying in bed. My mind will just start wandering, and this thought just kind of drifts in that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up the next morning. 

It's not that I want to actively do something to end my life, it's more just this overwhelming, heavy feeling of wanting to hit a permanent pause button on everything. The idea of just going to sleep and not having to wake up and face the phone ringing, or the incomplete notes, or that constant, crushing fear of letting everyone down again... it just sounds like such a relief in those moments. 

And then, almost immediately after I think it, it really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because working at the clinic, even just being around the administrative side of things, I know exactly what that can mean. I see it on the intake forms, I hear the clinicians talking about it—I know that wishing you wouldn't wake up is a massive warning sign. I know the trajectory of how those thoughts can escalate if you don't do something about them. So catching my own brain doing it, finding actual comfort in the idea of just slipping away in my sleep? It's like a massive red flag waving right in my face. I don't have a plan, but just the fact that my mind is going to that dark of a place to find an escape is a huge part of why I told my boss I needed help. It's just too scary to ignore when you know exactly what those kinds of thoughts represent.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving or worsening over time
doctor.question: Have your symptoms been getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past few weeks?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, since the clinic lost staff and my schedule shifted into late-evening coverage and heavier crisis paperwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression and timeframe of my symptoms over the past few weeks, which corresponds to the duration of my current episode.

patient.answer:
Worse. Definitely worse. It's... well, this whole thing really started about a month ago, and it feels like it's just been snowballing ever since. See, what happened was, we lost a couple of staff members at the clinic pretty suddenly. Just, boom, people were gone, and management was completely scrambling to figure out how to cover everything. So, my schedule got completely shifted around to fill the gaps, and they moved me into this late-evening coverage. 

And the evening shifts... I mean, it's just a totally different environment. The daytime is busy, sure, but the evening is when things get really intense. You start getting all these heavy, urgent calls, so suddenly I was drowning in all this heavier crisis paperwork. And with crisis documentation, you have to be so incredibly precise, because if you miss one detail, the consequences could be disastrous. You're documenting risk assessments, safety plans, all these things where you absolutely cannot afford to make a mistake. 

So that all started about a month ago, and at first, I just thought, okay, I'm just adjusting to the new hours, I'm just tired because my sleep schedule is off and I'm getting home so late. But it didn't get better. It just kept piling up, and my anxiety about the notes kept getting worse, and that's when I started freezing up on the phone, and then those dark thoughts started creeping in at night when I'd finally get home from those late shifts... so, yeah, over the past few weeks, it's definitely been getting worse. It's like every week I just feel a little more paralyzed by it all, just totally unable to handle the weight of it. I keep thinking maybe I'll get used to it, but the dread just keeps compounding instead.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are you still able to find pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: My guitar has been sitting in the corner, I keep bailing on soccer and the shelter, and even when I try to cook or go hiking it just feels like going through motions with no point to it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about my ability to find pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, which corresponds to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Pleasure? No... no, not really. Honestly, it feels like that part of my brain just completely shut off. 

Like, I have this acoustic guitar that I usually play all the time. It used to be my favorite way to decompress after a long day. But now it’s literally just been sitting in the corner of my bedroom collecting dust for weeks. I look at it, and I know I should play it, I know it used to make me feel good, but I just... I don't even want to touch it. The desire is just completely gone. 

And it's not just the guitar, it's everything. I play in this rec soccer league with some guys, and I usually love it, but I keep bailing on them. Every week they text me to see if I'm coming to the game, and every week I just make up some excuse about being too tired from my new schedule. I've been bailing on my volunteer shifts at the animal shelter, too. I've always loved dogs, they usually cheer me right up, but the thought of going in and putting on a happy face just feels impossible right now. I just can't bring myself to show up.

And the worst part is, even when I do manage to force myself to do something I usually like, it doesn't even work. Like, I’ll try to cook a decent meal instead of eating junk, or I’ll drag myself out to go hiking because I know I'm supposed to get outside and get some fresh air... but when I'm out there on the trail, or standing in my kitchen chopping vegetables, it just feels like I'm completely hollow. It just feels like going through the motions with absolutely no point to it. There's no spark, no satisfaction when the food is done or when I reach the top of the hill. I'm just physically there, doing the steps, waiting for it to be over so I can go back home. It’s incredibly frustrating because I know I used to love doing all of this stuff, and now everything, even my hobbies, just feels like a massive, pointless chore.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving
doctor.question: Have you noticed any improvement in your overall mental state since we started talking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any improvement in my mental state during our conversation, which does not map to any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Improvement? Um... no, honestly, I don't think so. I mean, we've been talking for a bit now, and I really appreciate you listening, I do. It's just... I still feel that same heavy weight sitting right in the middle of my chest. 

It's like, I was kind of hoping that just saying all this out loud to a professional might flip a switch, you know? Like maybe if I just got it all out on the table, all the stuff about the clinic and the crisis notes and those awful thoughts at night, that I'd suddenly feel this huge wave of relief. Because that's what we're supposed to tell people, right? That talking helps. But right now, I just feel... exhausted. Like I've just been digging through all this mud and now I'm just sitting here covered in it. 

I guess I'm still just as anxious about having to go back to work tomorrow and face that mountain of incomplete paperwork. The dread hasn't really lifted at all. I mean, maybe it takes more time, maybe I'm expecting too much from just one conversation, but right in this exact moment? No, I don't feel any better. I still just feel completely drained and overwhelmed by everything we've been talking about. I still just kind of wish I could go to sleep and not have to deal with any of it.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of persistent feelings of worthlessness, guilt, and suicidal ideation, along with a significant loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities and a decrease in appetite, point towards a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder.
